methodological_rigor.justification: This is a single-institution retrospective cohort of 215 patients with NCCN-defined very high-risk (n = 179) or regional (n = 36) prostate cancer treated with HDR brachytherapy plus EBRT from 2006–2022 (Abstract/Methods). The design can support descriptive outcome estimates and prognostic associations but is limited by retrospective selection, evolving practice over a 17-year window, and lack of a contemporaneous comparison group. The survival analyses use Kaplan–Meier methods and Cox regression with multivariable modeling to identify predictors such as pre-RT PSA > 0.1 ng/mL and cT4 disease (Abstract), which are appropriate for time-to-event endpoints as described.

clinical_relevance_loe.justification: This is an individual observational cohort study of real-world outcomes after combined-modality radiotherapy for very high-risk/regional prostate cancer, consistent with Oxford LoE 2b (Abstract). The endpoints (recurrence-free survival, cancer-specific survival, overall survival, and grade >= 3 toxicity) are directly patient-relevant and clinically interpretable (Abstract). The work is clinically relevant for counseling and risk stratification in a high-risk population, even though causal inference about HDR-BT benefit versus alternatives is not possible without a comparator.

reporting_quality.justification: As a retrospective cohort analysis, STROBE is the appropriate reporting framework (Abstract/Methods). The manuscript reports cohort size, calendar years, risk-group definitions, survival outcomes, multivariable Cox results with hazard ratios and p-values, and toxicity rates including grade >= 3 GU/GI toxicity (Abstract). However, key observational-reporting elements are not fully evident in the blinded text, such as detailed handling of missing data, clear patient-flow/exclusions, and prespecification of covariates and follow-up assessment. Data and code availability are not described; reproducibility relies on the narrative methods.

novelty_literature.justification: HDR-BT plus EBRT for high/very-high risk prostate cancer has an existing literature base, and the paper’s core design is a familiar retrospective outcomes series. The novelty is mainly in focusing the cohort on the revised NCCN very high-risk definition and including regional (cN1) patients over a long institutional experience (Abstract/Introduction). This is a meaningful but incremental contribution rather than a methodologically novel or practice-changing study.

writing_presentation.justification: The abstract clearly states the population, time window (2006–2022), sample size (n = 215), endpoints, and key multivariable findings (HRs and p-values). The introduction frames the motivation around the updated NCCN criteria and the uncertainty about outcomes in this subgroup. The presentation is generally clear and clinically oriented, with toxicity and survival outcomes described in standard terms.

key_strengths: Large single-institution experience (n = 215) with long-term follow-up for NCCN-defined very high-risk and regional prostate cancer (Abstract).
Clinically relevant endpoints including RFS/CSS/OS and reported grade >= 3 toxicity rates (Abstract).
Uses multivariable Cox regression to identify prognostic factors (e.g., pre-RT PSA > 0.1 ng/mL; cT4 disease) rather than only unadjusted outcomes (Abstract).
key_concerns: Retrospective, single-center design over a long calendar period with potential selection bias and unmeasured confounding; no comparator arm limits causal claims (Abstract/Discussion).
Potential practice changes from 2006–2022 (staging, imaging, systemic therapy) could affect outcomes and complicate interpretation across the cohort (Study period in Abstract).
Reporting details for exclusions, missing data handling, and follow-up definitions are not fully explicit in the blinded text.
chief_reviewer.rationale: This is a solid retrospective outcomes and prognostic-factor paper with substantial clinical relevance but limited by lack of a comparator and single-center design; it is plausibly acceptable in a Tier 3 journal with minor revisions to strengthen reporting clarity.
